title: 1 Samuel 18:6–16
context: The women of Israel greet the returning army singing that Saul has slain his thousands and David his ten thousands. Saul is angry and from that day watches David with suspicion. The next day an evil spirit from God comes on Saul; he raves in the house and twice throws his spear at David, who escapes. Saul fears David because the LORD is with David and has departed from Saul, so he sends David out as a commander, and all Israel and Judah love him. The song and Saul’s jealousy are told as narrative, not as commands. Verse 10 recalls 16:14 and needs care: both traditions affirm that God is sovereign even over spirits and judgment, that God is not the author of sin, and that Saul remains responsible for his envy and violence. They describe the relation between divine judgment and human sin in somewhat different terms, but they share these affirmations.

verses.text: As they came, when David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with instruments of music.
verses.arminianNotes:
As the army returns after David’s victory, women from all Israel’s cities come out singing and dancing to meet King Saul with tambourines, joy and instruments. A victory celebration greets the king.

Arminian readers note that public celebration of God’s deliverance is fitting, and that the scene begins in joy before Saul’s response turns it to envy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that women’s songs celebrating victory are known elsewhere in Israel’s story, as with Miriam (Exodus 15:20–21), and that the celebration rightly marks God’s deliverance, though it soon becomes the occasion of Saul’s sin.

Both traditions read the scene as narrative: a fitting celebration that exposes the condition of the king’s heart.

verses.text: The women sang to one another as they played, and said, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The women sing to one another, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” The song is repeated later, even among the Philistines (21:11; 29:5).

Arminian readers note that the song may be a poetic parallelism honoring both men rather than an intended insult, but Saul hears it as a comparison, showing how envy can twist innocent words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the song, whatever its intention, publicly proclaims David’s rise and becomes a refrain tied to his reputation; it is narrative, not a divine verdict, yet it fits what God is doing.

Both traditions read the song as reported speech that sets Saul’s jealousy in motion.

verses.text: Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul is very angry and displeased, saying they credit David with ten thousands and him with thousands, and asking what more David can have but the kingdom. Saul suspects David will take his throne.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s jealousy is his own sinful response, and that envy, once indulged, distorts his perception and leads him toward violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s suspicion unknowingly voices the truth that God has given the kingdom to another (15:28), but that Saul resists God’s decree rather than submitting to it, compounding his guilt.

Both traditions read Saul’s anger as narrative that shows envy’s destructive power and his own responsibility for it.

verses.text: Saul watched David from that day and forward.
verses.arminianNotes:
From that day on, Saul watches David with suspicion. The word suggests a jealous, hostile eye.

Arminian readers note that this is a turning point in Saul’s heart; he chooses suspicion over gratitude, and his continued choice of envy will steadily harden him against David and against God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s ongoing watchfulness is the fruit of a heart already turned from God, and that sin, left unrepented, binds a person more deeply over time, as the following chapters show.

Both traditions see the verse as narrating the beginning of Saul’s long hostility toward the one God has chosen.

verses.text: On the next day, an evil spirit from God came mightily on Saul, and he prophesied in the middle of the house. David played with his hand, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand;
verses.arminianNotes:
The next day an evil spirit from God comes mightily on Saul, and he prophesies in the house while David plays music as usual, and Saul has a spear in hand. The Hebrew verb is the one used for prophetic ecstasy; many translations render it raved.

Arminian readers note that the spirit comes as judgment on Saul’s persistent rebellion (15:23), and that God’s judgment never makes Saul’s envy or violence any less his own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s sovereignty extends even over evil spirits and over judgment, as in 16:14, while God is never the author of sin; Saul’s envy and violence remain his own. This verse and the next are commonly listed among those absent from the shorter Septuagint form.

Both traditions affirm God’s sovereignty over judgment and Saul’s real responsibility.

verses.text: and Saul threw the spear, for he said, “I will pin David to the wall!” David escaped from his presence twice.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul hurls his spear, intending to pin David to the wall, but David escapes from him twice. Saul’s jealousy turns murderous.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s attempt is a deliberate choice to act on his anger, and that David’s escape shows God’s protection of the one who trusted him, though David must also act to escape.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s preservation of his anointed is sure, and that David’s escapes, though involving his own quick movement, are the outworking of God’s protecting hand over his chosen king.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative of Saul’s sin and of God’s care for David.

verses.text: Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him, and had departed from Saul.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul is afraid of David, because the LORD is with David and has departed from Saul. The narrator gives the theological reason for Saul’s fear.

Arminian readers note that the LORD’s departure from Saul follows Saul’s repeated disobedience (13:13–14; 15:22–23), showing that persistent rebellion can lead to God’s withdrawal of favor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse frames the whole contrast between the two men in terms of God’s presence: everything turns on whom the LORD is with, which reflects his sovereign choice of David (16:13–14).

Both traditions see God’s presence with David as the decisive reality of the chapter, and see Saul’s fear as fear of what God is doing.

verses.text: Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul removes David from his presence and makes him commander of a thousand, and David goes out and comes in before the people. Saul’s attempt to distance David backfires.

Arminian readers note that Saul may hope to expose David to danger or simply to remove a rival from sight, yet the new post gives David greater visibility and influence with the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase going out and coming in before the people describes leadership in war, and that Saul’s own decisions unwittingly prepare David for kingship, as God overrules human intentions (compare Genesis 50:20).

Both traditions see God’s purposes advancing through Saul’s attempt to sideline David.

verses.text: David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the LORD was with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David acts wisely in all his ways, and the LORD is with him. The narrator again pairs David’s conduct with God’s presence.

Arminian readers note that David’s wise behavior and the LORD’s presence go together; God is with the one who walks faithfully, and faith is shown in the consistent choices of daily life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the statement “the LORD was with him” is the narrative’s explanation for David’s success, so that David’s wisdom is the fruit of God’s prior grace and presence.

Both traditions hold together David’s real faithfulness and God’s real presence, though they order the relation between them differently.

verses.text: When Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he stood in awe of him.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Saul sees how wisely David acts, he stands in awe of him. Saul’s fear deepens.

Arminian readers note that Saul recognizes the hand of God on David yet refuses to respond with humility or repentance, a tragic example of seeing God’s work and resisting it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s awe is not reverent submission but dread, the reaction of one who opposes what God is doing, and that recognition of God’s work does not by itself produce a changed heart.

Both traditions read Saul’s response as a warning about the difference between acknowledging God’s power and yielding to it.

verses.text: But all Israel and Judah loved David; for he went out and came in before them.
verses.arminianNotes:
But all Israel and Judah love David, because he goes out and comes in before them. David’s popularity grows across the nation.

Arminian readers note that David wins the people’s affection through faithful service and leadership, earned through conduct rather than demanded, which is a model for godly leadership.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the mention of both Israel and Judah anticipates the later united kingdom under David (2 Samuel 5:1–5), and that God is preparing the hearts of the people to receive their appointed king.

Both traditions see the people’s love for David as part of God’s work in raising him up.
